verses: When it was decided that we would sail to Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a man named Julius, a centurion of Augustus' army.
We boarded a ship at Adramyttium and set out, intending to sail along the coast of Asia; Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us.
The next day we arrived at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends to refresh himself.
When we set out from there, we sailed past Cyprus because the winds were contrary.
After sailing across the seas of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing to Italy, and he placed us on it.
When we had been sailing slowly for many days and had barely reached Cnidus, the wind would not let us go, so we sailed past Crete, opposite Salmone.
Just as we passed it, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
After a long time had passed and sailing became dangerous because the fast was already over, Paul warned them,
He said to them, 'Friends, I see that this voyage will bring injury and great loss, not only to the cargo and the ship but also to our lives.'
Nevertheless, the centurion trusted the ship's captain and owner more than the things Paul had said.
Since the harbor was not suitable for wintering, most advised leaving there as well, if they could reach Phoenix and winter there; it is a harbor in Crete, lying to the southwest and northwest.
When the south wind blew gently, thinking they had achieved their purpose, they set out and sailed close to Crete.
But soon a violent wind called Euroclydon arose against them.
When the ship was caught and could not sail into the wind, we let it drift.
As we passed under an island called Clauda, we had much work to do on the boat.
When they had hoisted it aboard, they used supports to undergird the ship; and, fearing they might run aground on the quicksands, they lowered the sail, and so were driven.
We were being tossed violently by the storm; the next day they lightened the ship.
On the third day we threw overboard the ship's rigging with our own hands.
When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and a great storm was upon us, all hope of being saved was taken away.
After a long period without food, Paul stood up among them and said, "Gentlemen, you should have listened to me and not set sail from Crete, avoiding this harm and loss."
Now I urge you to be of good cheer, for no one's life will be lost among you, only the ship's.
For an angel of God, whose servant I am, stood by me that night.
He said, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must be taken before Caesar, and look, God has given you all who are sailing with you."
Therefore, men, take heart, for I believe God that it will be just as it was told me.
However, we must run aground on a certain island.
But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were drawing near to some land.
And they took soundings and found it twenty fathoms; and when they had gone a little further, they took soundings again and found it fifteen fathoms.
Then, fearing that we might run aground on rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and wished for daylight.
And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship, when they had let down the lifeboat into the sea, under pretense as though they would lay out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, "Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved."
Then the soldiers cut off the ropes of the lifeboat and let it fall away.
And while the day was coming on, Paul urged them all to take food, saying, "Today is the fourteenth day that you have waited and continued fasting, having taken nothing."
Therefore I urge you to take some food, for this is for your survival; for not a hair shall fall from the head of any of you.
And when he had said this, he took bread and gave thanks to God in the presence of them all; and when he had broken it, he began to eat.
Then they were all encouraged, and they also took some food.
In all, there were two hundred and sixty‑six souls on the ship.
When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship and threw the wheat into the sea.
When daylight came, they did not recognize the land, but they observed a bay with a beach, into which they decided, if possible, to run the ship aground.
And when they had cast off the anchors, they left them in the sea, loosened the rudder ropes, hoisted the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore.
They came to a place where two seas met and ran the ship aground; the front part stuck fast and would not move, but the rear part was broken by the force of the waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so that none of them could swim away and escape.
But the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stopped them; he ordered those who could swim to jump into the sea first and reach the shore.
The rest clung to planks and broken pieces of the ship, and all of them safely reached land.
